The cable just snapped, forty floors up. Before you jump, you should know the elevator was built for this exact moment.
Elevators make eighteen billion passenger trips a year in America alone, and the number that plunge to the bottom is almost zero.
Your car hangs from four to eight steel ropes, and any single one of them can hold the entire cabin by itself.
Even if every rope failed, a speed governor trips a brake that bites into the guide rails, an idea from eighteen fifty three.
At the bottom of every shaft sits a buffer, a giant piston of oil or springs, built to catch a runaway car.
Instinct says jump at the last second, but you would need to leap upward at the car's full speed, which nobody can.
Lie flat on your back instead, arms and legs spread wide, so the impact spreads across your whole body and not your spine.
In nineteen forty five a bomber struck the Empire State Building and one elevator operator fell seventy five floors and survived.
She lived because the severed cables piled up beneath her car like a spring, and trapped air in the shaft slowed the fall.
The far likelier emergency is a stalled car, so press the alarm, use the intercom, and never force the doors open yourself.
Here is the twist, many passengers hurt by elevators were climbing out of a stuck car, not riding one that fell.
So if it drops, lie flat, and if it merely stops, sit down and wait, because the box is safer than the shaft.
